Methodology & Caveats

  • Source: USAspending.gov public award API, queried live — no bulk dataset was downloaded to produce this view.
  • Scope: Department of Defense as awarding agency, all award types, action dates 2024-10-01 through 2025-09-30 (FY2025).
  • The top 100 NAICS industry codes by dollar amount were retrieved (92.3% of total obligations) and grouped by hand into 18 mission-relevant categories; the remainder — the long tail of smaller NAICS codes plus grants, direct payments, and other non-contract assistance — is shown as Other.
  • This is an independently constructed taxonomy for analysis purposes, not an official DoD budget or appropriations classification (which uses Procurement / RDT&E / O&M / Military Personnel lines instead).
  • DoD contract awards carry a 90-day publication delay under federal disclosure rules, so the most recent weeks of FY2025 activity may be slightly underrepresented.

What this is: the top 30 DoD vendors by FY2025 dollar value, cross-referenced against how much of each vendor's spend falls under Census Bureau catch-all NAICS codes — industry classifications literally titled "All Other…" that get used when a business's work doesn't fit a more specific category.

What this is not: proof of waste, fraud, or mismanagement. A high catch-all share means the public classification data says less about what was purchased — nothing more. It is a starting point for deeper contract-level review, not a finding.

Methodology & Caveats

  • Source: USAspending.gov public award API, queried live. Vendors are ranked by total DoD-awarded dollar value for FY2025 (2024-10-01 through 2025-09-30), consolidated across registered entity-name variants (e.g. "Lockheed Martin Corp" and "Lockheed Martin Corporation" are combined).
  • Non-Specific Share = the portion of a vendor's DoD dollars classified under NAICS codes whose title begins with "All Other" (e.g. "All Other Professional, Scientific, and Technical Services"). These are Census Bureau catch-all classifications, used when a business's activity doesn't fit a more specific code — by definition, they disclose less about the nature of the work than a specific code would.
  • Computed from each vendor's top 50 NAICS codes by dollar amount; vendors flagged "additional codes not shown" have a longer tail beyond that cut — their true share may differ from what's shown here.
  • Vendors with only 1–3 total NAICS codes (e.g. many health-plan administrators, sole-source pharma distributors) are highly specialized, single-purpose contractors — a 0% non-specific share for them reflects a narrow business line, not a clean bill of health, and isn't comparable to a diversified prime's share.
  • This ranking does not indicate wrongdoing. Legitimate reasons a vendor's spend concentrates in catch-all codes include broad professional-services contracts, evolving scopes of work, or contracting-officer classification habits. Treat elevated shares as a prompt to pull the underlying contract records, not as a conclusion.
  • DoD contract awards carry a 90-day publication delay, so the most recent weeks of FY2025 activity may be underrepresented for all vendors.
i

Four procurement-pattern tests below. Three produced clean, usable findings. The fourth (threshold clustering) is shown anyway, with its result: it did not hold up as a reliable signal once checked properly, and we explain why rather than dressing it up.

Single-Bid "Competed" Contracts

Nominally competitive, functionally uncontested

A contract coded "full and open competition" can still draw only one bidder — often a sign of high barriers to entry, incumbent lock-in, or requirements written narrowly enough that only one company can realistically meet them. Scoped to definitive contracts specifically (where competition decisions are actually made, as opposed to orders placed under an already-competed vehicle). This required USAspending's bulk award-download data — the field isn't exposed through the standard search API.

Single-Bid Competed Contracts 3,098 of 10,986 genuinely-competed contracts
Share of Competed Contracts 28.2% by count
Total Value $17.5B 11.3% of competed-contract dollars
Top Vendor $1.2B Lockheed Martin Corporation, 20 contracts
More than a quarter of nominally-competed definitive contracts drew exactly one bidder. This spans the largest primes — Lockheed Martin alone accounts for $1.2B across 20 single-bid competed contracts — which fits a well-documented pattern in defense procurement: highly specialized, capital-intensive work (shipyards, classified systems, sustainment of legacy platforms) often has exactly one company capable of bidding, even when the solicitation is technically open to all. That's frequently a structural reality of the defense industrial base, not a procurement failure. It's still worth surfacing, because it's the same underlying condition GAO reports point to when they recommend agencies work to expand the industrial base or reconsider whether a requirement needs to be split into more competable pieces.

Drill-Down: Single-Bid Contracts Under the $350K Threshold

Near-threshold ($300K–$349,999)

Narrowing the single-bid pattern to contracts under the Simplified Acquisition Threshold — where competition requirements are lighter to begin with, so a single bidder is less inherently surprising, but still worth a look, especially where the award size sits conspicuously close to the $350K line.

559 single-bid competed contracts under $350K ($89.9M)
69 of those in the $300K–$349,999 near-threshold band ($22.2M)
Leland Limited Inc — Defense Logistics Agency (Navy/Marine supply) — 7 single-bid awards, same product, near-monthly cadence. Every one of Leland's FY2024–25 contracts with DLA was for Marine Lifesaving and Diving Equipment, ran $224K–$240K, was nominally competed under Simplified Acquisition Procedures, and drew exactly one bidder — Leland. That's consistent with a genuinely thin supplier market for specialized diving/marine-safety gear (in which case one bidder every time is simply reality, not a process failure) — but it's also exactly the pattern worth a contracting officer double-checking: are other qualified suppliers being notified of these solicitations, or is the sourcing list effectively down to one company by default?

Obligation Timing Across FY2025

Common government-spending folklore says agencies rush to obligate before the fiscal year ends in September ("use it or lose it"). That's not what DoD's FY2025 data shows.

Peak Month Dec '24 $92.3B, +125% vs. average
September (FY-End) -3% vs. average — essentially flat
Monthly Average $41.0B across 12 months of FY2025
Highest Non-Competitive Month 61% Mar 2025
December 2024 obligated 2.3× the monthly average — by far the largest month in FY2025, dwarfing September's fiscal year-end (-3% vs. average, i.e. essentially a normal month). The most common driver of a pattern like this is appropriations timing: DoD frequently operates under a Continuing Resolution at the start of the fiscal year, which restricts new-start spending until a full-year appropriations bill (often passed in December) unlocks it — producing a backlog release rather than a deliberate year-end rush. December and March also carried the highest non-competitive shares (53.9% and 60.9% of dollars, vs. ~40–52% in other months), consistent with obligations moving faster, with less time for competitive procedures, right after funding unlocks. This is a plausible explanation, not a proven cause — we have not traced individual December awards back to specific appropriations actions.

Cost-Reimbursement Exposure by Vendor

Cost-type shifts overrun risk to the government

Fixed-price contracts put cost-overrun risk on the vendor; cost-reimbursement contracts put it on the government. Neither is wrong — cost-type is standard (and often required) for FFRDCs, novel R&D, and unique sustainment work — but a vendor's mix is a useful risk profile, not a verdict.

$145.2B cost-reimbursement (29.5% of contract $)
$342.2B fixed-price (69.6%)
5 of the top 30 vendors are 100% cost-type
The five vendors at 100% cost-type are not a red flag — they're exactly who you'd expect: Humana Government Business and TriWest Healthcare Alliance administer TRICARE health plans (cost-reimbursement by design), Bechtel Plant Machinery and Fluor Marine Propulsion sustain naval nuclear reactors (unique, sole-source expertise), and Johns Hopkins APL is a federally funded R&D center (FFRDCs are structured as cost-type). Large primes cluster in the 30–75% range, reflecting their mix of production (fixed-price) and R&D/sustainment (cost-type) work. Nothing here indicates impropriety on its own — it's a map of where cost-growth risk sits, useful alongside other signals, not instead of them.

Threshold Clustering — Tested, No Reliable Signal Found

We looked for the classic "structuring" pattern: the same vendor receiving multiple awards from the same office on the same day, each individually under the $350K SAT, that together exceed it — a way to dodge the competition requirement on what should've been one larger, competed buy.

Initial pattern looked significant, but didn't hold up. We found 155 same-vendor/same-day/same-agency clusters across 8 candidate vendors, totaling $155.6M, even after excluding clusters that shared one existing parent supply vehicle (i.e. routine multiple calls under an already-competed contract, which is normal). But the two vendors driving nearly all of it — AmerisourceBergen Drug Corp (120 clusters, $121.7M) and Atlantic Diving Supply (21 clusters, $22.4M) — are large, established DLA distributors (pharmaceuticals and tactical/diving gear) who hold multiple concurrent supply IDVs as their normal operating model. Getting several separate calls from DLA on the same day, each against a different existing vehicle, is exactly what a high-volume distributor's business looks like — not evidence of splitting one requirement into two to dodge competition.

A genuinely reliable test would need to compare the item-level descriptions of same-day awards to check whether they're really the same requirement split in two — that data isn't available through USAspending's bulk API. We're reporting this as a tested-and-inconclusive result rather than either hiding it or overstating it.

Methodology & Caveats

  • Source: USAspending.gov public award API, queried live. Scope: Department of Defense, FY2025 (2024-10-01 through 2025-09-30), contract award types only.
  • Obligation timing uses actual (calendar) obligation month via each award's action date; "non-competitive" uses the same B/C/G extent-competed definition as the Vendor Concentration tab.
  • Cost-type mix uses FPDS contract pricing type codes: cost-reimbursement = Cost Plus Award Fee, Cost No Fee, Cost Sharing, Cost Plus Fixed Fee, Cost Plus Incentive Fee; fixed-price = Firm Fixed Price and its variants. Time-and-materials contracts (0.3% of dollars) are excluded from both buckets.
  • Threshold clustering was tested on the 8 vendors with the highest dollar concentration in the $300,000–$349,999 band; "same parent vehicle" is inferred from each award's underlying IDV/BPA reference number.
  • Single-bid competed contracts covers all 17,701 DoD definitive contracts (award type "D") for FY2025, pulled via USAspending's bulk award-download endpoint (the only place "Number of Offers Received" is exposed — it's absent from the standard search API). "Genuinely competed" = Full and Open Competition, Full and Open Competition after Exclusion of Sources, or Competed under Simplified Acquisition Procedures; sole-source categories are excluded since a single offer is expected by design for those. Branch in the drill-down table is the awarding sub-agency reported on the award (Army, Navy, Air Force, Defense Logistics Agency, and other DoD components) — not necessarily where the equipment or service is ultimately used.
  • A fifth analysis — small-business subcontracting pass-through — was investigated but not included on this tab: USAspending's subaward data can be reliably scoped to a specific prime contract (via its Award ID), but most prime awards have zero reported subawards at all (a known FSRS reporting-compliance gap), and there's no business-size field on subaward records, so classifying a subcontractor as "large" or "small" requires a separate lookup per subcontractor. Early spot-checks did not support a "small businesses fronting for large corporations" pattern — one high-pass-through case we found (97.5% of a $76M contract subcontracted) went to another small business, not a large one — but the coverage gaps mean this isn't reliable enough to present as a finding yet.
